title: Four forms of organisational sense making
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart's premise is that a school runs on the stories it tells about itself, that those stories guide thousands of daily decisions, and that the same event - a new policy, a dip in results, a parent complaint - can mean different things to different people until meaning fragments and cohesion goes. He names four forms organisational sense making can take. Guided sense making is the goal: shared understanding built through interpretation across a team, recognisable when staff can say what the priorities are and why, and when the improvement plan functions as a living purpose rather than a document. Getting there depends on leaders doing sense giving - anchoring purpose in narrative rather than in mission statements, and inviting interpretation because no one person sees the whole terrain. The three weaker forms each get symptoms, causes and a way back: restricted sense making, where meaning flows downward from hierarchy and staffroom talk is about deadlines rather than direction; fragmented sense making, where departments generate competing narratives and the school looks busy but incoherent; and minimal sense making, where fatigue has replaced interpretation with routine and the school's direction becomes accidental. The leader's job, he concludes, is to steward interactions and to notice which of the three is setting in.
points: Hart's diagnostic contribution is the typology itself - restricted, fragmented and minimal sense making each have distinct symptoms, so a leader can tell which failure they are in before prescribing.
The test for guided sense making is behavioural rather than documentary: can people explain what the priorities are and why they matter, and does practice talk connect to a coherent narrative.
He is explicitly sceptical of mission, vision and values statements, arguing they declare identity without creating the daily meaning-making that coherence actually requires.

Restricted sense making is traced to pressure - inspection, accountability cycles, fear of inconsistency - which is why he prescribes framing questions and short dialogue cycles rather than more directives.

Fragmentation is diagnosed as a connective-tissue problem following growth or well-meant empowerment without a shared interpretive frame, and minimal sense making as a capacity problem following overload.
quotes: Every school tells stories about itself that communicate who we are and what we value. Those stories guide thousands of small decisions every day. They are how people make sense of the work.

In schools, you know you’re in this territory when people can explain what the priorities are and why they matter. Conversations about practice connect to a coherent narrative. The improvement plan isn’t just a document; it’s a living sense of purpose that shapes daily choices.

Mission, vision and values statements promise clarity but rarely create coherence. They declare who we think we are but not how meaning is made in the day to day life of a school. Guided sense making begins when leaders turn intent into narrative.

Staff are told what decisions mean rather than invited to explore them. In this environment, people might understand what is happening but not why. The stories circulating in the staffroom and corridors are about deadlines and demands, not direction or purpose.

In fragmented sense making, initiatives multiply. A maths department might pursue mastery while English experiments with inquiry based learning; both valuable, but neither informed by the other. The organisation looks busy but feels incoherent.
Minimal sense making often follows overload or fatigue. When capacity is stretched, reflection feels like a luxury. The organisation’s cognitive bandwidth narrows until only the immediate survives.
